question: What is the purpose of a boat's capacity plate?
choice_a: It indicates the maximum weight capacity and maximum number of people the vessel can carry safely
choice_b: It lists the boat's resale value
choice_c: It records the date of the vessel's last oil change
choice_d: It shows the owner's insurance policy number
explanation: The capacity plate, usually mounted near the operator's station or on the transom, states the maximum weight and/or maximum number of persons the vessel can carry safely under normal conditions.
source_note: NASBLA-based boating safety curriculum used by AZGFD-approved course providers, 'Vessel Capacity'

question: What is a Hull Identification Number (HIN)?
choice_a: The horsepower rating of the vessel's engine
choice_b: A permanent, unique 12-character serial number molded or affixed to a vessel's hull that identifies it much like a VIN identifies a car
choice_c: The vessel's Arizona registration decal number
choice_d: A number the owner chooses and paints on the hull for decoration
explanation: A Hull Identification Number is a unique 12-character number assigned to a vessel by its manufacturer (or by AZGFD for homemade vessels), permanently affixed to the transom, that serves as the vessel's lifetime identifier for registration and title records.
source_note: NASBLA-based boating safety curriculum used by AZGFD-approved course providers, 'Hull Identification Numbers'

question: What is the key difference between a displacement hull and a planing hull?
choice_a: There is no meaningful difference between the two hull types
choice_b: A planing hull can never be used in open water
choice_c: A displacement hull pushes through the water and is limited in top speed by its waterline length, while a planing hull is designed to rise up and glide across the water's surface at higher speeds
choice_d: A displacement hull is only found on personal watercraft
explanation: Displacement hulls (common on sailboats, trawlers, and larger cruisers) push through the water and are speed-limited by their waterline length, while planing hulls (common on many powerboats) rise and glide across the surface as speed increases.
source_note: NASBLA-based boating safety curriculum used by AZGFD-approved course providers, 'Types of Hulls'

question: How is a personal watercraft (PWC) generally defined?
choice_a: Any small rowboat used for fishing
choice_c: A vessel that can only be operated by licensed captains
choice_d: A vessel less than 16 feet long that uses an inboard motor powering a water-jet pump as its primary source of propulsion and is designed to be operated by a person sitting, standing, or kneeling on it, rather than sitting or standing inside it
explanation: A PWC (personal watercraft, such as a Jet Ski or WaveRunner) is a vessel of less than 16 feet that uses an inboard motor powering a water-jet pump for propulsion and is operated by a person positioned on top of it rather than inside a hull.
source_note: NASBLA-based boating safety curriculum used by AZGFD-approved course providers, 'Personal Watercraft'

question: What is the difference between an outboard motor and a stern drive (inboard/outboard, or I/O) engine?
choice_a: An outboard motor is a self-contained unit mounted on the outside of the transom, while a stern drive combines an engine mounted inside the hull with an outdrive unit mounted outside the transom
choice_b: They are two names for the exact same type of engine
choice_c: An outboard motor is always larger than a stern drive engine
choice_d: A stern drive is only used on personal watercraft
explanation: An outboard motor is a self-contained propulsion unit clamped or bolted to the transom, while a stern drive (I/O) pairs an inboard-mounted engine with an outdrive/lower unit outside the hull that steers and propels the boat.
source_note: NASBLA-based boating safety curriculum used by AZGFD-approved course providers, 'Types of Engines and Drives'

question: On a boat, which direction is the 'bow'?
choice_a: The right side of the vessel when facing forward
choice_d: The left side of the vessel when facing forward
explanation: The bow is the forward, or front, part of a vessel; the stern is the rear, port is the left side facing forward, and starboard is the right side facing forward.
source_note: NASBLA-based boating safety curriculum used by AZGFD-approved course providers, 'Vessel Terminology'

question: Which side of a vessel is the 'port' side?
choice_a: The very back of the vessel
choice_c: The left side when facing the bow (front)
choice_d: The right side when facing the bow (front)
explanation: Port is always the left side of a vessel when facing forward toward the bow; starboard is the right side. These terms do not change no matter which way the operator is actually facing.
source_note: NASBLA-based boating safety curriculum used by AZGFD-approved course providers, 'Vessel Terminology'

question: Why does the traditional federal length-class system (Class A: under 16 ft; Class 1: 16 to under 26 ft; Class 2: 26 to under 40 ft; Class 3: 40 to under 65 ft) matter to a recreational boater?
choice_a: It determines the color the hull must be painted
choice_b: It sets the minimum age of the operator
choice_c: It determines which specific lake the vessel may be used on
choice_d: A vessel's length class determines which safety equipment -- such as fire extinguishers, lights, and sound-signaling devices -- it is required to carry
explanation: The federal vessel length classes underlying most state and NASBLA-based course material determine what equipment -- number of fire extinguishers, navigation lights, sound-producing devices, and more -- a vessel must carry to comply with the law.
source_note: NASBLA-based boating safety curriculum used by AZGFD-approved course providers, 'Vessel Length Classes'

question: Do PWC and some other small vessels typically have a capacity plate like a conventional boat?
choice_a: No -- PWC and some other vessels are not required to carry a capacity plate, so operators should follow the capacity recommended in the owner's manual and on the manufacturer's warning decal
choice_b: Yes, every PWC has a capacity plate identical to a larger cruiser
choice_c: No, PWC have no weight or passenger limit at all
choice_d: Yes, but only PWC manufactured before 1990
explanation: PWC and certain other vessels are not required to display a capacity plate. Instead, operators should follow the maximum capacity recommended in the owner's manual and on the manufacturer's warning decal.
source_note: NASBLA-based boating safety curriculum used by AZGFD-approved course providers, 'Vessel Capacity'

question: For registration and equipment purposes, how does Arizona law generally treat a personal watercraft?
choice_a: As safety equipment rather than a vessel
choice_b: As a motorized watercraft that falls under the same general vessel requirements as any other boat, with additional PWC-specific rules layered on top
choice_c: As exempt from nearly all boating regulations
choice_d: As a non-motorized vessel similar to a canoe or kayak
explanation: Under Arizona law, a PWC is a motorized watercraft subject to the same general registration, equipment, and operating requirements as other vessels, plus a set of additional rules written specifically for PWC operation.
source_note: A.R.S. Title 5, Chapter 3 boating statutes and NASBLA-based course material, 'Personal Watercraft'
